passage: For decades, municipal water treatment facilities and industrial plants have treated wastewater primarily as an environmental hazard to be cleaned and discharged at considerable expense. Increasingly, however, environmental engineers view used water not as waste, but as a concentrated reservoir of valuable resources. Modern recovery systems can extract phosphorus and nitrogen from sewage sludge to manufacture slow-release agricultural fertilizers, reducing reliance on mined mineral reserves. Simultaneously, anaerobic digesters break down organic matter to capture biogas—a renewable methane fuel capable of powering the treatment facility itself—while advanced membrane filtration purifies water to drinking-grade standards for urban reuse. By transforming treatment plants into circular resource-recovery hubs, cities cut operational costs, lower greenhouse gas emissions, and build resilience against severe droughts.
